inline.s: The various bodies wrought by mind—I say this is mind-only.
Bound by the habit-energy of false imagining, all things arise from mind;
Beings see them as external—I say this is mind-only.
What is seen outside does not exist, yet mind displays all manner of things;
Body, wealth, and dwelling-place—I say this is mind-only.”

At that time Mahāmati Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha: “World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has said: ‘As I have taught, you and all bodhisattvas should not rely on the words and grasp their meaning.’ World-Honored One, why should one not rely on the words and grasp the meaning? What are words? What is meaning?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, as for words: their cause is the habit-energy of discrimination, and relying on throat, tongue, lips, palate, teeth, and gums, they bring forth all manner of sounds, letters, and phrases, speaking to one another—this is called words. What is meaning? A bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells alone in a solitary, quiet place, and by the wisdom of hearing, reflecting, and cultivating, he contemplates and observes the path to nirvāṇa, the realm of his own wisdom; he turns about the habit-energies and courses in the various aspects of the bodhisattva grounds—this is called meaning. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is skilled in words and in meaning, and knows that words and meaning are neither one nor different, and that meaning in relation to words is likewise so. If meaning were different from words, then meaning should not be made manifest through words; but it is through words that meaning is seen, as a lamp reveals visible form. Mahāmati, just as a man holds up a lamp to illumine things and knows that this thing is thus and is in such a place, so too the bodhisattva mahāsattva, by the lamp of words and speech, enters the realm of self-realization beyond words. Furthermore, Mahāmati, if one grasps the meaning according to the words in regard to non-arising and non-ceasing, intrinsic nature, nirvāṇa, the three vehicles, the one vehicle, the five dharmas, and the self-nature of all the minds and so forth, then one falls into the views of affirmation and of denial, because one discriminates in a way contrary to that; it is like taking an illusion for real—this is the view of the foolish, not that of the noble ones.” At that time the World-Honored One again spoke in verse:
“If one grasps the meaning following after words, one constructs all dharmas;
By that construction, at death one falls into the hells.
Within the aggregates there is no self, yet the aggregates are not the self;
The foolish discriminate thus, yet it is neither nonexistent either.
As the foolish discriminate, all things possess a nature;
If it were as they see it, then all should see the real.
All dharmas, defiled and pure, are wholly without a nature of their own;
It is not as they see it, nor yet are they utterly nonexistent.

“Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now set forth for you the marks of wisdom and of consciousness. If you and all bodhisattvas mahāsattvas understand well the marks of wisdom and consciousness, you will quickly attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi. Mahāmati, there are three kinds of wisdom, namely: worldly wisdom, supramundane wisdom, and the supreme supramundane wisdom. What is worldly wisdom? It is the reckoning of being and non-being by all the tīrthikas and ordinary folk. What is supramundane wisdom? It is the clinging of all the two vehicles to self-marks and common-marks. What is the supreme supramundane wisdom? It is the Buddhas and bodhisattvas contemplating all dharmas as wholly without marks, neither arising nor ceasing, neither existent nor nonexistent, realizing the egolessness of dharmas and entering the Tathāgata ground. Mahāmati, there are again three kinds of wisdom, namely: the wisdom that knows self-marks and common-marks, the wisdom that knows arising and ceasing, and the wisdom that knows non-arising and non-ceasing. Furthermore, Mahāmati, arising and ceasing is consciousness; non-arising and non-ceasing is wisdom. Falling into marks and marklessness, and into the various marks and causes of being and non-being, is consciousness; being free from marks and marklessness and from the causes of being and non-being is wisdom. Having the marks of accumulation is consciousness; having no marks of accumulation is wisdom. Clinging to the marks of objects is consciousness; not clinging to the marks of objects is wisdom. Arising from the meeting and conjunction of the three is consciousness; the mark of self-nature arising in unobstructed accord is wisdom. Having the marks of attainment is consciousness; having no marks of attainment is wisdom. The realm realized by the noble wisdom within oneself is like the moon in water: because it neither enters nor emerges.”
“Gathering karma is mind; observing dharmas is wisdom,
Wisdom realizes the markless, and attains sovereign majesty of light.
Bound by objects is mind; wisdom is what arises in awakened thought;
In the markless and in the surpassing, wisdom arises within.
Mind, mental, and consciousness, apart from all discriminating thoughts;
He who attains the undiscriminated Dharma is a Buddha-son, not a śrāvaka.
The supreme, still quiescence-patient, the Tathāgata’s pure wisdom;
Born of the excellent, supreme meaning, far removed from all that is practiced.
I have three kinds of wisdom, which the noble ones can clearly illumine,
Discriminating among all marks, revealing all dharmas,
My wisdom is free of all marks, and far surpasses the two vehicles.
Because the śrāvakas and the rest cling to the existence of all dharmas;
The Tathāgata’s wisdom is stainless, for he comprehends mind-only.

“Furthermore, Mahāmati, the tīrthikas hold nine kinds of views of transformation, namely: transformation of shape, transformation of mark, transformation of cause, transformation of correspondence, transformation of view, transformation of birth, transformation of thing, transformation of the clarity of conditions, and transformation of the clarity of what is done; these are the nine. Because of these views, all the tīrthikas set up doctrines of the transformation of being and non-being. Among these, the transformation of shape means the view of shape as distinct and different: for example, when gold is made into ornaments, into rings, bracelets, and necklaces, all manner of different things, the shapes differ but the substance of the gold does not change; the transformation of all dharmas is likewise so. All the various reckonings and clingings of the other tīrthikas are neither thus nor yet different; it is only because of discrimination that all is transformed—so should it be understood. For example, when milk, curds, wine, and fruit ripen, the tīrthikas say that all these have transformation; yet in truth there is neither being nor non-being, because what is seen is only one’s own mind and there is no external thing. All such as these are foolish, deluded ordinary folk, arising from their own habit-energy of discrimination; in truth not a single dharma is either born or ceases, like the forms seen in an illusion or a dream, like the child of a barren woman of whom one says that there is birth and death.”
“Transformation of shape, place, and time, of the elements and the faculties;
The intermediate existence arises by degrees—this is false imagining, not wise knowledge.
The Buddhas do not discriminate dependent arising and the world;
But the world of conditions is like a city of gandharvas.”

At that time Mahāmati Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha: “World-Honored One, I pray the Tathāgata to explain for me the profound secret meaning of all dharmas, and the marks of understanding that meaning. Let me and all bodhisattvas mahāsattvas understand this Dharma well, so that we do not fall into the profound clinging of grasping the meaning according to words, and are free from the vain discrimination of letters and speech; so that we may enter everywhere into all Buddha-lands, sealed by the powers, the superknowledges, and the dhāraṇīs; so that our awakened wisdom may dwell well in the ten inexhaustible vows, and by effortless effort display all manner of transformations, with light illumining as do sun and moon, mani, earth, water, fire, and wind; so that dwelling on the various grounds we are free from the view of discrimination; so that knowing all dharmas to be like an illusion and a dream, we enter the Tathāgata’s rank and universally transform beings, causing them to know all dharmas as vain and unreal, to be free from the categories of being and non-being, to cut off the clinging to arising and ceasing, and not to cling to words and speech, and so turn about their support.”

The Buddha said: “Listen well, and I shall tell you. Mahāmati, the profound clinging that grasps the meaning of all dharmas according to the words is immeasurable in number, namely: clinging to marks, clinging to conditions, clinging to being and non-being, clinging to arising and non-arising, clinging to ceasing and non-ceasing, clinging to vehicles and non-vehicles, clinging to the conditioned and the unconditioned, clinging to the self-marks of ground after ground, clinging to the self-discriminated realization, the tīrthikas’ clinging to the categories of being and non-being in their doctrines, and clinging to the three vehicles and the one vehicle. Mahāmati, these secret clingings are immeasurable in kind; they are all the secret clinging of ordinary, foolish folk to their own discrimination, and these discriminations are like a silkworm making its cocoon, wrapping itself and others with the silk threads of false imagining, clinging to being and non-being with a firm and secret delight. Mahāmati, herein there is in truth no mark of secret or non-secret, because the bodhisattva mahāsattva sees all dharmas as dwelling in stillness, and is without discrimination. If one comprehends that all dharmas are only what the mind sees, that there is no external thing, and that all alike are markless, and observes in accord with this, then in regard to the secret clinging of discrimination upon being and non-being, one sees all as still; therefore there is no mark of secret or non-secret. Mahāmati, herein there is no bondage and no liberation either; it is only those who do not understand the truth who see bondage and liberation. Why? Because in all dharmas, whether being or non-being, no essential nature can be found. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the foolish, deluded ordinary folk have three kinds of secret bondage, namely: greed, hatred, and delusion, and the craving for future birth together with greed and delight. By these secret bondages beings are made to continue being born in the five destinies; if the secret bondage is cut off, then there is no mark of secret or non-secret. Furthermore, Mahāmati, if one clings to the meeting and conjunction of the three, the secret bondage of the consciousnesses arises in succession. Because of clinging there is secret bondage; but if one sees the three liberations and is free from the consciousness of the three in conjunction, then all secrets do not arise at all.”
“Unreal, false discrimination—this is called the mark of the secret;
If one can know it as it really is, all the nets of secrets are cut.
The foolish cannot comprehend it, and grasp the meaning following after words;
Like a silkworm within its cocoon, by false imagining they bind themselves.”

At that time Mahāmati Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha: “World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has said: ‘It is through various minds that all dharmas are discriminated; it is not that dharmas possess a self-nature—this is merely false reckoning.’ World-Honored One, if it is merely false reckoning and there are no dharmas, would not all dharmas, defiled and pure, then be wholly destroyed?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, so it is, so it is, as you have said. All ordinary, foolish folk discriminate all dharmas, but the nature of dharmas is not as they suppose; this is merely false clinging, without nature or mark. Yet the noble ones, with the eye of noble wisdom, know and see as it really is that dharmas possess a self-nature.”

Mahāmati said: “If the noble ones, with the eye of noble wisdom, see that dharmas possess a nature, not with the divine eye nor the fleshly eye, and not as the foolish discriminate—how then can the foolish become free from discrimination? It is because they cannot awaken to the noble Dharma. World-Honored One, they are neither inverted nor non-inverted. Why? Because they do not see the Dharma seen by the noble ones; because the noble vision is far removed from the marks of being and non-being; because the noble ones do not attain as the foolish discriminate; because it is not the mark of the realm in which they move. They too see a nature and marks of dharmas, because these appear as the nature of false clinging; because it is not said that there is a cause or no cause; because they fall into the view of the nature and marks of dharmas. World-Honored One, since their other realms are not the same as this, there would then be the fault of endlessness—who could know the nature and marks of dharmas? World-Honored One, the nature and marks of dharmas do not depend upon discrimination; why then do you say that dharmas exist because of discrimination? World-Honored One, the marks of discrimination differ and the marks of dharmas differ; since the causes are not alike, how can dharmas come about from discrimination? And for what reason, though the discrimination of the foolish is not so, is it said: ‘In order to cause beings to abandon discrimination, it is taught that the marks of dharmas as seen in discrimination are not thus’? World-Honored One, why do you cause beings to be free from the dharmas clung to by the views of being and non-being, and yet again cling to the realm of noble wisdom, falling into the view of being? Why do you not speak of the Dharma of stillness and emptiness, but speak of the matter of the self-nature of noble wisdom?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, it is not that I do not speak of the still and empty Dharma, falling into the view of being. Why? Because I have spoken of the matter of the self-nature of noble wisdom. Because beings, from beginningless time, reckon and cling to being, I speak of the still Dharma by way of the noble matter, so that when they hear it they may not give rise to terror, but may truly realize the still and empty Dharma, be free from confused marks, enter the principle of consciousness-only, know that what they see has no external dharmas, awaken to the three gates of liberation and attain the seal of reality, see the self-nature of dharmas and understand the noble realm, and be far removed from all clinging to being and non-being. Furthermore, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not establish that all dharmas are wholly non-arising. Why? Because all dharmas are originally nonexistent, and because of the reason and the marks of arising of that thesis. Furthermore, Mahāmati, that all dharmas are non-arising—this statement destroys itself. Why? Because that thesis depends upon something and arises; and because that thesis is itself included within all dharmas, the mark of non-arising being also non-arising; and because that thesis is made up of various parts; and because that thesis holds that both being and non-being are non-arising, and this thesis is itself included within all dharmas, the marks of being and non-being being also non-arising. Therefore the thesis that all dharmas are non-arising destroys itself. One should not establish it thus, because the parts have many faults, and because the marks of causes in succession differ. As with non-arising, so too is it with the emptiness and egolessness of all dharmas. Mahāmati, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should teach that all dharmas are like an illusion and a dream, because of seeing and not seeing, and because all are marks of confusion—except that for the foolish it gives rise to terror. Mahāmati, the foolish, deluded ordinary folk fall into the views of being and non-being; do not cause them to be frightened and terrified and so turn away from the Great Vehicle.”
“No self-nature, no speaking, no thing, no place of reliance;
The foolish falsely discriminate, their evil notions like a corpse.
That all dharmas are non-arising is what the tīrthikas establish;
Because the arising they hold is not produced by conditions.
That all dharmas are non-arising, the wise do not discriminate;
Because their thesis arises from a cause, this notion is then destroyed.
As when the eye has a cataract, one falsely imagines hairs and a wheel in the air;
So too are all dharmas—the foolish falsely discriminate.
The three realms are but names, with no real substance of dharmas;
From these names and constructs, discrimination falsely reckons and measures.
The marks of things that are but names disturb the mind-consciousness;
The Buddha-sons wholly transcend them, and walk in non-discrimination.
Where there is no water they take the mark of water—this arises from thirsty craving;
So the foolish see dharmas; the noble ones do not.
The noble ones see purity, and are born into the three liberations;
Far removed from arising and ceasing, they ever walk in the markless realm.
Cultivating the markless realm, there is neither being nor non-being;
Being and non-being are wholly equal, and so the noble fruit is born.
How do dharmas come to be or not to be? How is equality accomplished?
If the mind does not comprehend dharmas, within and without there is confusion;
Once comprehended, then there is equality, and the marks of confusion cease at that time.”

At that time Mahāmati Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha: “World-Honored One, as the Buddha has said: if one knows that the objective realm is merely names and wholly unobtainable, then there is nothing grasped; because there is nothing grasped, there is also no grasping; and since both the grasping and the grasped are absent, discrimination does not arise—this is called wisdom. World-Honored One, why is it that this wisdom does not obtain the object? Is it because it does not comprehend the meaning of the one and the different in the self-marks and common-marks of all dharmas, and so is said not to obtain it? Or is it because the self-marks and common-marks of all dharmas, being various and different, conceal one another, and so it does not obtain it? Or is it because it is covered and separated by mountains, rocks, cliffs, curtains, veils, and screens, and so does not obtain it? Or is it because of extreme distance or extreme nearness, of youth or age, of blindness or darkness, or of the faculties being incomplete, that it does not obtain it? If it is because it does not comprehend the meaning of the one and the different in the self-marks and common-marks of all dharmas, and so is said not to obtain it, then this should not be called wisdom; it should be no-wisdom, because there is an object and yet it does not know it. If it is because the self-marks and common-marks of all dharmas, being various and different, conceal one another, and so it does not obtain them, this too is not wisdom, because it is the knowing of an object that is called wisdom, and not the not-knowing of it. If it is because of being covered and separated by mountains, rocks, cliffs, curtains, veils, and screens, or because of extreme distance or extreme nearness, of youth or age, of blindness or darkness, that it does not know, that too is not wisdom, because there is an object and yet wisdom is not complete and so does not know it.”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, this is truly wisdom, and it is not as you suppose; what I have taught is not a teaching of concealment. When I say that the objective realm is merely names and unobtainable, it is because one comprehends that it is only what one’s own mind sees, and that the being and non-being of external dharmas is something in which wisdom in the end finds nothing to obtain; because there is nothing to obtain, the objects of cognition do not arise, and entering the three gates of liberation, the very substance of wisdom is forgotten. It is not as with all the ordinary folk of awakened notions, who from beginningless time have been perfumed by conceptual elaboration, and who reckon and cling to external dharmas as being or non-being in all their various forms and marks; such knowing as theirs is called not-knowing, for they do not comprehend that all dharmas are only what the mind sees, and clinging to self and possessions they discriminate realm and wisdom, and do not know whether external dharmas are existent or nonexistent, their minds dwelling in the view of annihilation. In order to cause them to abandon such discrimination, I teach that all dharmas are established by mind only.”
“If in regard to an object of cognition, wisdom does not observe it;
That is not wisdom but no-wisdom; such a one is called a false reckoner.
Marks without bound conceal one another, and there are obstacles, and far and near;
That wisdom cannot see them is what is called wrong wisdom.
The aged and the young whose faculties are dim, though objects truly exist;
Cannot give rise to wisdom—this is called wrong wisdom.

“Furthermore, Mahāmati, foolish, deluded ordinary folk, from beginningless time, are deluded by vain and false, evil and crooked discrimination; they do not comprehend the teaching of truth itself nor the teaching of words, and reckoning the marks outside the mind, they cling to skillful means of speech, and cannot cultivate the pure and real Dharma that is free from the four alternatives.”

Mahāmati said: “So it is, so it is, truly as the Venerable One teaches. I pray you to explain for me the Dharma of truth itself and the Dharma of words, so that I and all bodhisattvas mahāsattvas may gain skill in these two dharmas, which the tīrthikas and the two vehicles are unable to enter.”

The Buddha said: “Listen well, and I shall tell you. Mahāmati, the Tathāgatas of the three times have two kinds of Dharma, namely: the teaching of words and the teaching of truth itself. The teaching of words is the various skillful teachings spoken according to the minds of beings. The teaching of truth itself is this: the practitioner, in regard to what is manifested by the mind, is free from all discrimination, does not fall into the categories of one and different, both and neither, transcends all mind, mental, and consciousness, and in the realm of the noble wisdom of self-realization is free from all marks of the views of causes, conditions, and correspondences; it cannot be known by all the tīrthikas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas who fall into the two extremes—this is called the teaching of truth itself. These two kinds of Dharma you and all bodhisattvas mahāsattvas should well cultivate and learn.”
At that time the World-Honored One again spoke in verse:
“I teach two kinds of Dharma: the teaching of words, and truth itself;
The teaching of words is shown to ordinary folk; truth itself is for the practitioner.”

At that time Mahāmati Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha: “World-Honored One, the Tathāgata once spoke of the mantras and treatises of the Lokāyatas, which can only win worldly wealth and gain, and do not win the gain of Dharma; and since they do not win the gain of Dharma, one should not draw near to them, serve them, or make offerings to them. World-Honored One, why did you speak thus?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, all the treatises of the Lokāyatas merely adorn their phrases and sentences to deceive and confuse ordinary, foolish folk; they accord with the vain speech of the world, do not accord with the meaning, do not fit the principle, cannot lead to the realization of the real realm, cannot awaken one to all dharmas, and ever fall into the two extremes, so that one loses the right path oneself and causes others to lose it too, revolving through the destinies with never any escape. Why? Because they do not comprehend that all dharmas are only what the mind sees, and clinging to outer objects they increase their discrimination. Therefore I say that the phrases and sentences of worldly treatises, adorned with reasons and similes, merely deceive the foolish, and cannot free one from the woes of birth, old age, sickness, and death, of sorrow and grief. Mahāmati, Śakra, lord of the devas, broadly understood all the treatises and composed treatises himself. A certain disciple of those holders of worldly treatises manifested a dragon body and came to Śakra’s heavenly palace, where he set up his thesis and made this solemn declaration: ‘Kauśika, let me debate with you. If you are not my equal, I shall break your thousand-spoked wheel; if I am not your equal, I shall cut off my head one by one in acknowledgment of my defeat.’ Having spoken these words, he at once overcame Śakra by the method of debate and shattered the thousand-spoked wheel, and then returned to the human world. Mahāmati, the treatises of the world, adorned with reasons and similes, can go so far as to manifest a dragon form and by fine phrases and words delude the devas and asuras, causing them to cling to views of arising and ceasing—how much more so human beings! Therefore, Mahāmati, one should not draw near to them, serve them, or make offerings to them, because they can produce the causes of suffering. Mahāmati, the worldly treatises speak only of the realm of bodily sensation. Mahāmati, those worldly treatises have hundreds of thousands of words and phrases; in later ages, evil views will be estranged and divided, the crooked multitudes will break apart, split into many schools, each clinging to its own causes. Mahāmati, it is not other tīrthikas who can establish a teaching; only the Lokāyatas, with hundreds of thousands of phrases, broadly set forth immeasurable and various marks of causes, which are not the truth itself, and they themselves do not know that this is a Dharma that deludes the world.”

At that time Mahāmati said: “World-Honored One, if the treatises composed by the Lokāyatas, with all their various letters, reasons, and similes, are adorned with words, and cling to their own theses and are not the truth itself, they are called tīrthikas. But the World-Honored One also speaks of worldly matters, saying that with all manner of phrases and words he broadly tells of the assemblies of devas and humans from all the lands of the ten directions who come together, which is not a Dharma realized by his own wisdom. Does the World-Honored One then speak as the tīrthikas do?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, I do not speak as the world does, nor do I come or go; I teach that all dharmas neither come nor go. Mahāmati, coming is gathering and arising, going is perishing and ceasing; neither coming nor going—this is what is called non-arising and non-ceasing. Mahāmati, what I teach is not the same as the tīrthikas, who fall into discrimination. Why? Because I am unattached to the being and non-being of external dharmas; because I comprehend that it is only one’s own mind and do not see the two graspings; because I do not move in the realm of marks and do not give rise to discrimination; and because I am liberated by entering the gates of emptiness, marklessness, and wishlessness. Mahāmati, I recall that once, when I was dwelling in one place, a brahmin of worldly treatises came to where I was and abruptly asked me: ‘Gautama, is everything made?’ I answered at once: ‘Brahmin, that everything is made is the first worldly treatise.’ He asked me again: ‘Is everything not made?’ I answered at once: ‘That everything is not made is the second worldly treatise.’ He asked again: ‘Is everything permanent? Is everything impermanent? Is everything born? Is everything unborn?’ I answered at once: ‘That is the sixth worldly treatise.’ He asked again: ‘Is everything one? Is everything different? Is everything both? Is everything neither? Does everything receive birth from various causes and conditions?’ I answered at once: ‘That is the eleventh worldly treatise.’ He asked again: ‘Is everything ascertainable? Is everything unascertainable? Is there a self? Is there no self? Is there this world? Is there no this world? Is there another world? Is there no other world? Is there liberation? Is there no liberation? Is it momentary? Is it not momentary? Are space, nirvāṇa, and non-selective cessation made or not made? Is there an intermediate existence? Is there no intermediate existence?’ I answered at once: ‘Brahmin, all such as these are your worldly treatises; they are not what I teach. Brahmin, I teach that the three realms arise from the various evil habit-energies of beginningless conceptual elaboration, and that not comprehending that they are only what one’s own mind sees, one grasps external dharmas, though in truth nothing can be obtained. As the tīrthikas say, ‘I,’ the faculties, and their objects—the three in conjunction—produce knowledge; I do not speak thus. I do not speak of a cause, nor do I speak of no cause; it is only by way of the false mind appearing as grasper and grasped that I speak of dependent arising, which neither you nor others who grasp at a self can fathom.’ Mahāmati, space, nirvāṇa, and non-selective cessation have only the number three and originally no substantial nature; how much less can one say of them that they are made or not made.

“Mahāmati, at that time the brahmin of worldly treatises asked me again: ‘Is it because of the causes and conditions of ignorance, craving, and karma that there are the three realms? Or is it without cause?’ I said: ‘These two are also worldly treatises.’ He asked me again: ‘Do all dharmas enter into self-marks and common-marks?’ I answered at once: ‘This too is a worldly treatise. Brahmin, even if there is but the slightest movement of mind-consciousness discriminating outer objects, it is all a worldly treatise.’ Mahāmati, at that time that brahmin asked me again: ‘Is there anything that is not a worldly treatise? All the treatises of all the tīrthikas, with their various phrases, sentences, reasons, and similes, do they not all come forth from my Dharma?’ I answered: ‘There is. It is not what you allow, nor is it disallowed by the world; it is not that I do not speak of various phrases and sentences that accord with the meaning and principle, nor that I do not speak of those that do not accord.’ He asked again: ‘Can there be something allowed by the world that is not a worldly treatise?’ I answered: ‘There can. But it is not something that you and all the tīrthikas can know. Why? Because you falsely discriminate external dharmas and so give rise to clinging. If one can comprehend that dharmas such as being and non-being are all only what one’s own mind sees, and does not give rise to discrimination and does not grasp outer objects, then one dwells in one’s own place. To dwell in one’s own place is not to arise; not to arise in what? Not to arise in discrimination. This is my Dharma, and it is not yours. Brahmin, in brief, wherever the mind-consciousness comes and goes, in birth and death, seeking and yearning, whether feeling, seeing, touching, or dwelling, grasping all manner of marks and continuing in conjunction, giving rise to clinging to craving and to causes—all of that is your worldly treatise, not my Dharma.’

“Mahāmati, when the brahmin of worldly treatises asked me thus and I answered thus, he did not ask me about the real Dharma of my own teaching, but departed in silence, thinking: ‘The ascetic Gautama is worthy of no respect; he teaches that all dharmas are unborn, markless, without cause or condition, and are only what one’s own mind discriminates and sees, and that if one can comprehend this, discrimination does not arise.’ Mahāmati, you too now ask me this meaning—why is it that by drawing near to the holders of worldly treatises one wins only the gain of wealth and not the gain of Dharma?”
Mahāmati said: “What is the meaning of the wealth and the Dharma you speak of?”

The Buddha said: “Excellent! You are able to ponder this meaning for the sake of beings in the future. Listen well, listen well, and I shall tell you. Mahāmati, as for wealth: it can be touched, felt, grasped, and tasted, it causes one to cling to outer objects and fall into the two extremes, and it increases craving, birth, old age, sickness, and death, sorrow, grief, and affliction. I and all the Buddhas call this the gain of wealth, and it is what is obtained by drawing near to worldly treatises. What is the gain of Dharma? It is to comprehend that dharmas are the mind’s seeing and the two egolessnesses, not to grasp at marks and to be without discrimination, to know well the various grounds and be free from mind, mental, and consciousness, to be consecrated in common by all the Buddhas, to fulfill and practice the ten inexhaustible vows, and to gain mastery in all dharmas—this is called the gain of Dharma; by this one does not fall into the two extremes of permanence and annihilation, which are the discrimination of all views and conceptual elaborations. Mahāmati, the worldly treatises of the tīrthikas cause foolish people to fall into the two extremes, namely, permanence and annihilation: receiving the doctrine of no cause, they give rise to the view of permanence; when the cause perishes and ceases, they give rise to the view of annihilation. I say that one who does not see arising, dwelling, and ceasing is one who has gained the benefit of Dharma—this is called the marks of the difference between wealth and Dharma. You and all bodhisattvas mahāsattvas should diligently observe this.”
“To tame and gather beings, and by discipline to subdue all evil;
By wisdom to extinguish all views, and so to increase liberation.
What the tīrthikas vainly say is all worldly disputation;
Falsely reckoning maker and made, they cannot stand on their own.
Only my own one teaching does not cling to the grasped and the grasper;
For the sake of all the disciples I teach it, that they may be free of worldly disputation.
The dharmas of the grasped and the grasper are mind-only, without anything that exists;
Both kinds are manifested by mind; permanence and annihilation cannot be found.
Even the moving of the mind—that is worldly disputation;
He in whom discrimination does not arise is one who sees his own mind.
When a thing comes, one sees it arise; when it goes, the thing is no more;
Clearly knowing coming and going, one does not give rise to discrimination.
Permanence and impermanence, the made and the unmade;
This world and the next, and the like—all are dharmas of worldly disputation.”

At that time Mahāmati Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha: “World-Honored One, the Buddha speaks of nirvāṇa—what dharma does he take as nirvāṇa, seeing that the tīrthikas each discriminate it in various ways?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, as the tīrthikas discriminate nirvāṇa, none of them accord with the marks of nirvāṇa. Listen well, listen well, and I shall tell you. Mahāmati, some tīrthikas say that when one sees dharmas as impermanent and does not crave objects, and the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields cease, so that the dharmas of mind and mental factors no longer appear before one, and one does not think on the objects of past, present, and future, it is like a lamp gone out, like a seed rotted, like a fire extinguished, and the graspings do not arise and discrimination is not born—this they conceive as nirvāṇa. Mahāmati, it is not by the destruction of views that it is called nirvāṇa. Or they say that reaching a certain region is attaining nirvāṇa, the marks of objects being left behind as when the wind ceases. Or they say that not perceiving the perceiver and the perceived is called nirvāṇa. Or they say that not giving rise to the views of permanence and impermanence in discrimination is attaining nirvāṇa. Or some say that the marks of discrimination give rise to suffering, and that not knowing this to be what one’s own mind manifests, out of that not-knowing they dread marks and seek marklessness, and deeply delighting in it, they cling to it as nirvāṇa. Or they conceive as nirvāṇa that one awakens to the self-marks and common-marks of all dharmas inner and outer, past, future, and present, as having a nature that does not perish. Or they reckon that the self, the person, beings, and lifespan, and all dharmas, are without destruction, and conceive this as nirvāṇa. Again, some tīrthikas, lacking wisdom, reckon that there is a self-nature, and that the puruṣa and the guṇas transform and make all things, and take this as nirvāṇa. Or some tīrthikas reckon that merit and demerit are exhausted, or that the afflictions are exhausted without wisdom, or that the sovereign lord is the real maker, and take this as nirvāṇa. Or they say that beings are born from one another in succession, and that this is the cause with no other cause; because they lack wisdom they cannot awaken to it, and not comprehending it they cling to it as nirvāṇa. Or they reckon that realizing the truths of the path is nirvāṇa, by false discrimination. Or they reckon that the guṇas and the possessor of the guṇas are conjoined, of one nature or of different nature, both or neither, and cling to this as nirvāṇa. Or they reckon that all things arise from nature of themselves—the hues of the peacock, the sharpness of the thorn, and the place where jewels are born bringing forth all kinds of gems; who is it that makes such things? They simply cling to nature itself as nirvāṇa. Or they say that one who understands the twenty-five principles thereby attains nirvāṇa. Or some say that receiving the six parts and protecting beings is attaining nirvāṇa. Or some say that time produces the world, and that time itself is nirvāṇa. Or they cling to something existent as nirvāṇa. Or they reckon nothingness as nirvāṇa. Or there are those who reckon both something and nothing as nirvāṇa. Or they reckon that all things are not different from nirvāṇa, and conceive this as nirvāṇa. Mahāmati, there is again what is different from what those tīrthikas teach: proclaimed with the lion’s roar of the one who knows all, it is to comprehend that all is what mind-only manifests and not to grasp outer objects, to be far removed from the four alternatives and dwell in the view of truth itself, not to fall into the two extremes and to be free from the grasped and the grasper, not to enter into the measures and not to cling to the real, to dwell in the Dharma realized by noble wisdom manifested within, to awaken to the two egolessnesses, to be free from the two afflictions, to purify the two kinds of obstruction, to turn about and cultivate the various grounds and enter the Buddha ground, to attain the great samādhis such as the illusion-like and so forth, and forever to transcend mind, mental, and consciousness—this is called attaining nirvāṇa. Mahāmati, the vain reckonings of those tīrthikas do not accord with the principle and are abandoned by the wise; they all fall into the two extremes and conceive nirvāṇa thereby. In this there is neither dwelling nor emerging; those tīrthikas all give rise to false notions according to their own theses, contradict the principle and accomplish nothing, and only cause the mind-consciousness to run scattered to and fro; none of them attains nirvāṇa. You and all the bodhisattvas should keep far away from all this.”
“The tīrthikas’ views of nirvāṇa, each with its own separate discrimination;
These are but false imagining, with no means of liberation.
Far removed from all means, they do not reach the place of no bondage;
They falsely give rise to the notion of liberation, yet there is no liberation.
What the tīrthikas establish, the many wisdoms each grasp differently;
None of them has liberation, but only foolish, false discrimination.
All the deluded tīrthikas falsely see maker and made;
They all cling to being and non-being, and therefore have no liberation.
The foolish delight in discrimination and do not give rise to true wisdom;
Words are the root of the three realms; the real is the cause that ends suffering.
As an image in a mirror, though it appears, is not real;
In the mind-mirror of habit-energy, the foolish see duality.
Not comprehending that it is mind-only manifest, they give rise to twofold discrimination;
If one knows it is only mind, then discrimination does not arise.
Mind itself is all manner of things, far removed from the imagined and the imagined marks;
As the foolish discriminate, though they see, they do not see.
The three realms are only discrimination; all outer objects are wholly nonexistent;
